faq.a: A light year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres. It measures distance, not time.
asks: How long is a light year?

faq.a: Apart from the Sun, it is Proxima Centauri, a small dim red star about 4.2 light years away, too faint to see without a telescope. Its bright neighbours, Alpha Centauri A and B, are only slightly further.
asks: Which star is closest to Earth?

faq.q: How do astronomers measure the distance to stars?
faq.a: For nearby stars they use parallax: as Earth moves round the Sun, a near star seems to shift slightly against more distant ones. The smaller the shift, the further away the star. The Gaia spacecraft has measured over a billion stars this way.

faq.q: Are we seeing stars as they are now?
faq.a: No, we see them as they were when their light set off. A star 500 light years away appears as it was 500 years ago, so looking out into space is looking back in time.
asks: Could a star I see already be gone?

faq.q: How long would it take to travel to the nearest star?
faq.a: With today's spacecraft, tens of thousands of years. The Voyager 1 probe, travelling about 17 kilometres per second, would take over 70,000 years to cover that distance.
asks: Could we fly to another star?

facts: Light travels about 300,000 kilometres per second and takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth from the Sun.
Proxima Centauri, the nearest star to the Sun, is about 4.24 light years away.
One light year is about 9.46 trillion kilometres.

quiz.why: A light year is the distance light travels in a year, so light from a star 4.2 light years away takes 4.2 years to arrive.

wrong.0: A jet plane would take about 5 million years.
wrong.1: A light year measures distance, not age; stars are millions or billions of years old.
